utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Laurie Sartorio for the Prosecution, assisted by Alma Imamovic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Sartorio. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson this morning on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Our case manager is Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Before I turn to the witness, let me just say that, unfortunately, Judge Harhoff is involved in another case this morning, and we are forced to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Saric. I hope I won't be too long with you this morning. If we could start off by briefly returning to two documents that we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Please, could we bring up Exhibit 858 onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, this is a document that we looked at several times during the course of your testimony. We can see that it is a report dated the 23rd of July, 1995, going from the 3rd Corps Military Security Service to the General Staff Security Administration. And we can say, first of all, you explained in your evidence that you didn't prepare this document, and you hadn't seen it before; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we can see, from the first paragraph of this document, it explains that in the course of combat operations on the 22nd of July, 1995, the El Mujahedin Detachment captured 11 enemy troops; and below that we can see the names of three of those troops are mentioned. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to ask you about is on -- it's on the second page in the English version, and it's the second-from-bottom paragraph on the B/C/S version. What this says, in this paragraph, it notes the El Mujahedin Detachment does not allow the aggressor soldiers to be taken over. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we can put this document away and turn to Exhibit 859 that we have also looked at during the course of Mr. Saric's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, we see here another document from the 3rd Corps Military Security Service to the General Staff Security Administration, and we can see that it's dated the 25th of July, and it was received at the security administration on the 28th of July. Do you remember seeing this document, Mr. Saric?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you recall, Mr. Saric, that you actually prepared this document that was sent to the security administration?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please have a look at the last page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could please turn to the last page in the B/C/S version, it's on page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could please return back to the start of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in the sequence of documents that the Trial Chamber has seen, this was the next document that was sent to the General Staff Security Administration concerning the captured Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could just slowly click through the pages in B/C/S, just so that we could refresh the witness as to what's contained in this document, and if we could move to the next page, please. It's not necessary for the witness to read the whole content, but just for him to see what the document consists of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Saric, we can see that this is a substantial document containing a lot of detailed information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could return back to page 1 in the B/C/S version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Saric, that nowhere in this document that you prepared does it actually say when the interviews took place with the Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your testimony, we ascertained that there is no mention of any mistreatment towards the Serb prisoners in the document. What I would like to ask you is this: Without you providing any details of the dates that these Serb prisoners were interviewed and this information was obtained, would you agree with me that anybody reading this document could gain the impression or understand from the document that interviews had taken place at some stage after the 23rd of July, when the first document about these Serb detainees was sent?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand what you mean, that it would have taken place after the 23rd or immediately before the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: After, Your Honour. I'll clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Saric, we saw that the first document in the sequence of the documents was sent on the 23rd of July. This document was sent on the 25th of July and received by the security administration on the 28th. On the face of this document, from looking at it, it's possible that someone reading the document could understand that the Serb detainees were interviewed subsequent to the first document being sent on the 23rd of July; in other words, it could have been later on the 23rd of July, it could have been the 24th, or even the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to understand why you say so, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is my position: We cross-referenced the dates on these documents to see when they were actually produced. We shall realise that those are roughly -- not roughly, but in fact quite certainly the very dates that Mr. Robson is referring to. We are talking about the time period between the 23rd and 25th of July, 1995, meaning the dates these reports and documents were produced are the 23rd, 24th, or the 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand all that, but you're still not giving me any reason why, on a reading of this document, the impression is given that the interview took place sometime after the 23rd or after the document of the 23rd. I'll tell you why I don't understand. I understand this document to be a document reporting to the General Staff what the 3rd Corps received from the 35th Division, and that the document of the 23rd was a document from the 35th Division. Now, this document says: "In the interview with the captured aggressor's ..." Now, I haven't read this whole document. These exhibits are flipped through quickly. We don't read them through, but it says here in the first paragraph: "In the interview with the captured aggressor's soldiers, the 35th Division of the Army learned the following information." Now, you are not telling the recipient of this document when the 35th Division did the interview, but you are telling him of what the 35th Division found. Yes, what the 35th Division learned. Therefore, the interview, to the reader of this document, is that the interview could have taken place shortly before the report from the 35th Division was written. That's as best I can understand it. I don't understand why you say "after the 23rd." The reader may not know when the 35th Division did the interview, but the impression left with the reader is that it took place before the report was given to you at the 3rd Corps shortly after the interview. Otherwise, how do you report on an interview that has not yet taken place? That's why I asked you the question right at the beginning and you said you were going to clarify, so I still don't understand your logic, the two of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robson, if you occasionally looked towards me, you would notice that I wanted to intervene. I'd also like to add that I find this somewhat problematic, especially with regard to the fact that Mr. Robson is asking questions on the witnesses rather with regard to possibilities rather than facts. I think we should focus the questions on facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could just, first of all, go back to the question that I put to the witness. As I understood the witness's answer, he wasn't saying that the interview did take place after the 23rd but he allowed that possibility, that it could have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's just what I can't understand, how it could have taken place after the 23rd. The reader of this document -- sorry. The reader of this document is not given, at least on this first page, the date when the 35th Division conducted the interview. Okay? But what the reader is told here, he is told that what is being reported by the 3rd Corps is what the 3rd Corps received from the 35th Division. Now, what the 35th Division reported to the 3rd Corps could only have taken place shortly before the report, not after the report. How can you report about something that has not yet taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm trying to explore with the witness, and if he doesn't know the answer, I'd be very grateful if he tells us so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But on the face of these two documents, the documents do not exclude the possibility that the Serbs were approached on two different occasions: The first occasion which was altered in the first document, the 23rd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Show us those two possibilities from the document. Refer us to a writing in the document which gives that impression because, otherwise, we don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't give testimony about the -- I don't wish to testify about the documents. What I'd like to do is just deal with this point; and if you're not satisfied, I'll move on. But what I'm trying to explore with the witness, I'll put this in a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, in the first document that we saw, dated the 23rd of July, it stated that the El Mujahedin Detachment did not allow the aggressor soldiers to be taken over, and we can see that there was very limited information in that document. We then have a document which was sent to the General Staff Security Administration two days later, containing a lot of detailed information. What I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to understand what is the limited information in the first document and what is the detailed information in the subsequent document which is not there in the first document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we can look at the documents and ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But ask him questions. Show us the details in the subsequent documents that are not there in the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, let's have a look at Exhibit 858, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can just scroll down a little in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, we can see that this is a one-page document. Would you agree with me that the information contained in this document about the Serb prisoners is restricted to the paragraphs 1, 2, and 3, which gives some brief information about the dates of birth of the prisoners, what their position is within the army, what their profession is, and maybe some other small pieces of information?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And now if we can have a look at Exhibit 859, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In this document, we can see that it starts off by giving similar information about the three named Serb prisoners: Their dates of birth, position within the army, some other information. Then the document goes on to, if we go --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you could have a look at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It explains about the line of defence that was controlled by the Prnjavor Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can turn over in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It then goes on to explain who the military commanders are within that brigade. It explains how various military units were -- what they were comprised of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can turn over in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is that correct, what I've said so far, Mr. Saric?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The document then goes on to explain about Howitzers being positioned near to a school, there is information about Chetniks manning trenches, and then you can see there's information about desertion amongst the Serb forces and so on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then we can see that there's a lot of detailed information about Dr. Branko Sikanic. He explains about the medical facilities in the area, and he goes on to explain about the general situation existing in the Ozren-Vozuca area; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So what we can see here, Mr. Saric, is that there was a lot of detailed information that just wasn't present in the that initial short report on the 23rd of July. What I was trying to explain -- or what I was trying to put to you was that somebody reading this subsequent report, because there is no date mentioned as to when this detailed information was obtained, could obtain the impression that subsequent information had been obtained from the Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, before the answer, because, again, this is calling for sheer speculation, asking this witness what someone else thinks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to answer this objection. In keeping with Rule 94 (H) -- it seems there is no interpretation. All right. Your Honours, in keeping with Rule 94 (H), I think, we are expected to put our case to the witness and hear what the witness has to say. Therefore, this is precisely what we, the Defence, have been doing, and we are expecting an answer from the witness. It's not about eliciting speculation. It's about hearing the witness's opinion with regard to our case in this particular instance. The Chamber can choose what its position is regarding certain documents when deliberations start. It may rate one document more and another document less, in terms of probative value. However, it is our responsibility to put our case to the witness in relation to each and every document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, this witness, as I understand, is not an expert witness, and Madam Vidovic is saying that it is not about speculation. It's about hearing the witness's opinion with regard to your case. Now, Judge Lattanzi has just said a little earlier that the question is being speculative and can we stick to facts. Any amount of speculation can come into where this information comes from. We don't know whether this report by the 3rd Corps to the General Staff is a combination of the report from the 35th Division and other reports, because there are all people, Karadzic, who are mentioned here, who are not mentioned outside, Vukmanovic, Popovic, Cikorac. They are all mentioned here, and we don't know where this information comes from. So there is any number of speculation as to why this report is longer than the other report. I do think this question is speculative, and I uphold the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just ask one question which doesn't call for speculation, and then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, in relation to the second document we've seen, dated the 25th of July, are you able to help me: Is there any reason why you didn't include the date of when the interview with the Serb prisoners, which resulted in this detailed information, was not included in the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand "which resulted in this detailed information," unless you're asking for the dates when the various information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, you obtained information; and as a result of receiving that information, you produced a document dated the 25th of July. You did not include, within that report, details of when the interview or interviews were conducted with those named Serb prisoners. Are you able to recall, is there any reason why you did not include details about when those Serb prisoners were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only reason that no information regarding the date the interviews were conducted with these POWs was included in my report, or at least my initials appear on the face of the document, is probably that the security organ of the 35th Division didn't include that information in their own report which they sent to us. Therefore, I was in no position to speculate on the exact dates of those interviews. Information that had reached us from the 35th Division was copied from the report and forwarded to the Security Administration of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you able to recall - and if you can't, please say so - did you receive information on two occasions from the 35th Division about these Serb prisoners before you prepared the report dated the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I see that there are two documents here; however, I truly cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move away from this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask the witness a few questions on this subject. Can we put on Exhibit 858, please. Could we put Exhibit 858 on the screen. Okay. Thank you. You may proceed now. I don't have any questions, as I see where this document comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could show the witness Exhibit 694, please. While we're waiting for the document to appear, if I could just explain that this is a report dated the 19th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, would you agree that we can see that this is a document from the 3rd Corps Military Security Service to the General Staff Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could look at the last page in B/C/S, please, and page 6 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that, in the signature block, the document is from Agan Haseljic. Can you confirm that you are the author of this document, Mr. Saric?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author of this document, judging by the initials, is me. However, it was signed by the head of the security service of the 3rd Corps, Colonel Agan Haseljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see his name is on the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could we please revert back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at paragraph 1, could you confirm for us that in this document, Colonel Haseljic is reporting to the General Staff Security Administration that, in the liberation of Vozuca, the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina captured a total of 39 aggressor soldiers and three female civilians in the period between the 10th of September and the 5th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It then goes on to say that all captured aggressor soldiers and civilians were taken to the Zenica Reception Centre and were interviewed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember this document? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if you'd like to look through the document in detail, if you'd like to scroll through it or see a hard copy, then please say so. But can you confirm for us that, within this document, there is no mention that any of the aggressor soldiers or civilians were held by the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we turn over the page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, there is no such a mention made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could show the last page in the B/C/S version, just so that he can look through that page and confirm that there's no information there. The second page, I beg your pardon, in the B/C/S. Your Honours, I think it's probably better if I give the witness a hard copy so he can check that thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When going through this report, one can state that there is no mention or description, for that matter, of any captured aggressor soldiers being held at the El Mujahedin camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, can you confirm that there is no mention within this report that any of those aggressor soldiers or civilians were mistreated by anybody at all?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, it is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the final issue I'd like to deal with deals with events in September 1995. From your testimony that you gave yesterday, Mr. Saric, as I understand it, you did not interview any Serb prisoners of war that had been detained by the El Mujahedin Detachment, with the exception of Mile Gojic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you interviewed Mr. Gojic at the Reception Centre at Zenica KP Dom; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Please, could we look at Exhibit 671. While we're waiting for the report to -- the document to appear, if I could just state for the record that this is a report dated the 1st of October, 1995. It's headed: "Results of interview with prisoners of war Mile Gojic and Nebojsa Banjac." If we could just look at the final page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saric, I don't see your initials on this document. Do you know, were you the author of the document or were you involved in it at all?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author of the document is my work-mate, Mehmed Siljak. I can see that by the initials. I was present on another occasion when the war prisoner Gojic, Mile, was interviewed, and I also spoke to him during a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could return back to the first page, please, and if I could ask you to look through the document briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, if you'd like to see a hard copy, I'd be happy to give you a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can do that, as the version on the screen is rather illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you've had a chance to read that document. I know you didn't prepare it, but could you confirm for us that nowhere in that document does it state that either Mile Gojic or Mr. Banjac sustained mistreatment at the hands of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're asking me about something I didn't have much to do with; however, from this report, it is clear that that was not the case, or rather, that the two prisoners of war were not mistreated or tortured, at least there's nothing of that sort mentioned in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your evidence yesterday, you were asked about Mile Gojic, and you commented upon the fact that he converted to Islam. You were asked by the Prosecutor if you knew why that was, and your response, as I recall, was that it was through fear. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that nowhere in this report does it state that Mile Gojic was placed in the situation of fear, which caused him to convert his religion to Islam?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can put this document away, and I'll turn to another document relating to Mile Gojic. It's Exhibit 779.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saric, we've seen this document before. Can you confirm that this is a report concerning a visit by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment to Mile Gojic, and the report is dated the 6th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, you told us that you were the author of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can look at page 2 in the B/C/S version and the final page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I recollect your testimony well, you told us that this document was a little bit strange or unusual. Can you confirm that we can see that the signature block has a line through it in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. That is precisely what I mentioned yesterday, I believe. I said that the initials were mine, and that we find there the name of the assistant commander for security, Colonel Agan Haseljic. However, the name and title are crossed out, and I believe I mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that there's no signature. But can you also confirm that if we look at the document, there is no stamp or markings to indicate that this document was ever sent or received?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see that it is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that for us to be certain that this document was sent, it would have to bear either the signature of Mr. Haseljic or somebody signing for him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. It should be signed and stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it may be that in looking at this document, in fact, all we're looking at is a draft or a working document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very or highly likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And one last point on this document. It was put to you by the Prosecutor, when you were asked questions about it, that this document indicated that Mr. Gojic and the other Serb detainees had been held from the 17th of September up until the 5th of November, and you were asked to comment about that. Now, if I could direct your attention to the first paragraph of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the first page in English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we look towards the bottom of the first paragraph, would you agree that this report shows that Mile Gojic was captured by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment on the 17th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second page in the English version, and I believe it's still on this page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you see, if you look down through the document, that it states quite clearly ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we're looking five lines down from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: ... it states that on the 30th of September, 1995, together with a group of captured aggressor soldiers, Mile Gojic was taken to the Zenica Centre for the Reception of Prisoners of War? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it in the English; however, I don't see it in the B/C/S. Oh, now I do. Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, in fact --

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the fifth line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, in fact, would you agree with me that this document clearly shows that Mr. Gojic and the other aggressor soldiers were released on the 30th of September and not the 5th of November, as was suggested to you in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I think you've already confirmed this document clearly shows that Mile Gojic and the other aggressor Serb soldiers were released on the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can move away from this document, and I'll turn to my final document. For this, if we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As a general comment, just to avoid confusion, may I suggest that we use the word "author" with reference to the person who signed the document, and "drafter" with reference to the person whose initials appear on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, I have a short redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, with regard to that last document that you were shown, - and I won't mention any names so we don't have to go into closed session - but after the signing of the agreement and the release of those persons, did you ever hear from any one of those persons again?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the course of your duties, did you use the packet system of communication, if you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, I do know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if you use the packet communication system, would that -- would there be a stamp or a signature that would be on the document that's transmitted electronically?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There has to be a signature, that much is certain. I'm not sure about the stamp, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So the signature is encrypted, it goes through the system? That's your opinion, that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, in order for a document to be sent through the system in an encrypted form, it would have had to be signed by the chief of the military security service; otherwise, it could not have been passed along in that form.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. But on the receiving end, when something is sent through the packet system, can you see a signature on a document on the receiving end?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume not. I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked some questions on cross-examination about - and, again, I'm not going to name names - but about interviews with females. You stated at one time --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Maybe we should go into closed session. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand the question of documents; but unless I know or the Chamber knows from which document that was not previously put in, the question arises and then the question still remains: Why ask the question now? Why wasn't it asked in chief? That's my question, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My response, Your Honour, is that -- and again I don't -- I'm not comfortable arguing about this in front of the witness. Perhaps the witness could remove his headphones. Would that be appropriate or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is asked to remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness mentioned or indicated that he understands English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Well, the implication of the cross-examination is that because certain information was not contained in reports, that there's no information that goes up. That is what this redirect is addressing. So it's a direct question in direct response to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that, Madam Sartorio. What I don't understand is why address that through an interview that you had when the witness arrived in The Hague, before the witness took the witness stand, and that which took place between you and him at that time was not put before court in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll just ask him the question direct, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask the question direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, at the time, back in 1995, in July, August, and September, if you had known that POWs were in the custody and detention of Mujahedin or El Mujahedin Detachment members, would this have caused you concern?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Sartorio, I'm having trouble with this question. It's not the question of whether or not it flows from the cross-examination, because, of course, there is a link to the cross-examination. But you are not asking the witness on what he would have done but on a possible concern he may have had, and I'm having problems with this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think maybe there will be a follow-up question, depending on his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But maybe you could invert the order of your questions. Maybe you could go directly to the facts and maybe not to the possible concerns he may have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Because the fact is, in response to what Your Honours suggested that we ask what he had done, perhaps that is -- I'll ask that question, Your Honour, first, if that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, in 1995, in July and August and September, if you had known that POWs were in the custody and detention of Mujahedin or El Mujahedin Detachment members, what action might you have -- would you have taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. We've heard from this witness that he knew that the prisoners of war had been in detention or in the hands of Mujahedin. We've heard that from him, so perhaps Prosecuting counsel could rephrase the question or ask a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic [sic] -- I'm so sorry. I'm sorry to her, in her absence. Madam Sartorio, you heard what the objection was. Can you respond to the objection, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I believe he knew after the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After which fact?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: After the fact that they were in the custody. I'm asking him if he knew -- the question is: When he found out or the minute he found out they were there, what action he would have taken. I think the documents show he may have known -- well, strike that. I just don't -- at this point I'm asking the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, if you stuck to the facts, you'd probably not be having these difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm not having difficulties, Your Honour. I wanted to ask the witness some questions about general knowledge, and that's where I started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this witness told you that he knew that these people were in Livade, in an El Mujahid Detachment detention centre. Is that so, sir? Is that what you said? That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can ask him based on that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. May I proceed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, when you found out the prisoners were in Livade, in the El Mujahedin Detachment detention centre, did you take any action to try to get them removed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were POWs that I was to interview, and that's all I wanted to know about them. What I was supposed to do was to inform my superior, if he didn't already know. But I don't think it's possible that he would not have known because this is an area that he was in charge of monitoring, I mean developments in that area. Therefore, I believe that what I did was the most I could have done, considering the situation. Anything else would have been within someone else's remit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, would it be convenient to carry on with this topic after the break? We are already five minutes into the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do so, can we just inquire after Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, she's in the Defence room, and I'm told that she's feeling better, but she felt extremely dizzy a moment ago and that's why she had to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hope she gets better and she can join us when we resume at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just say to you, Madam Vidovic, that I hope you are better. Please, if you at any stage feel the Trial Chamber must stop, please say so; or if you want to go out, feel free to go out. Mr. Robson, are you still cross-examining, or are you done? Madam Sartorio, yes, you were asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I was. Thank you, Your Honour, just a few questions more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, the last question I asked you is if you did anything when you learned the POWs were in the custody of the El Mujahedin, and you said that you did the most that you could, considering the situation. "Anything else would have been within someone else's remit." That was your answer. Do you remember giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My next question to you is: Regardless of the fact that you -- well, strike that. You claim that you did all that you could that was within the realm of your job duties; but outside that, personally, were you -- did you have concern about POWs in the custody of the El Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I wonder if some sort of time frame could be put on this question, if indeed it's appropriate, because this witness has explained that he has seen prisoners of war who were detained by the Mujahedin on a number of different occasions. So the prosecuting counsel has asked, "When were you concerned?" I think it's right that we put some sort of -- establish some sort of basis as to when it is that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll put a time frame, Your Honour, but I think I prefaced all of these questions with "July and August and September of 1995." I put that to the witness, and I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, in July, August, or September of 1995, did you have personal concern if you knew that POWs were in the custody of El Mujahedin or members of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally - I mean personally, which means I'm talking about myself - I was concerned, but it turned out, at least when I saw them, when I interviewed them, that they had been treated fairly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But my next question is: Personally you were concerned. What was this concern based on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how this arises out of the cross-examination, and therefore I object.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think we've already covered that objection, Your Honour. I'm asking him what information he had, and what his concern was based on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Madam Sartorio, as much as the Chamber doesn't want to interfere, but what does concern us is that you're asking the witness about his personal concerns and not what he did in his capacity as an operative within the system. I'm not quite sure what his personal concerns have to do with the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I totally agree, Your Honour, that his personal concerns aren't directly relevant to the issues in the case. It's what his personal concerns are based upon that may be relevant in the case. Information may be relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What he could and couldn't do is based on what he told us, the constraints in his position. They're two different -- there are two different concepts here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But shouldn't you have -- okay. Shouldn't you have solicited that information while you were leading the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, Your Honour, how to answer that question without going back over the direct, but this has come up in response to the direct attack on -- or the direct confrontation on documents that didn't contain information. I'm asking him about information that he may have had outside of the documents. So I believe it's directly relevant and in direct response to the cross-examination. I will accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may be, but I'll tell you what my concern is. You were aware of those documents, and you were aware that those documents that went up didn't have the information that was in the documents that came to him. So why you didn't deal with them yourself at that time, I do not understand, and now you want to deal with them because they were raised by cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's what redirect is about, though, Your Honour, is responding to points that are raised during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, points that are raised during cross-examination that were unforeseeable to you. Okay. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- ask the question. Let's just hear what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, with regard to your personal concerns, can you tell us what those personal concerns were based upon?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal concerns, which is the way you term it, were based on rumours that I had heard up to that point, but nothing official. The treatment, allegedly, was like that, well, what shall we call it, inhumane. However, any persons I spoke to, upon their arrival in the POW Reception Centre, told me that this had, in fact, not been the case. I even had an organised form of cooperation with some of those, which is what we discussed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. One more question, sir: Did you have a conversation with Mr. Vlajcic with regard to the POWs being in the custody of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that Mr. Osman Vlajcic, my boss, was in charge of and monitoring the Mujahedin issue, and given the fact that we had received official reports on the names of POWs being held in their detention, we spoke about the right way to interview them once they were brought into the POW Reception Centre in Zenica. We also said that I would probably be needing assistance, someone being seconded to me, one of my associates, operatives perhaps, to help me conduct interviews, since I would hardly have been able to handle all of that myself. Some of the documents show just that, show Siljak, my associate, as being a person who helped me, who quite physically did me a favour, because he agreed to interview some of those prisoners. As for any other activities or issues, I don't remember us ever discussing anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sartorio. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two questions to ask this witness. First of all, about Mile Gojic, Witness, if I'm not mistaken, you told us during the cross-examination today that in September 1995, the only prisoner whom you interviewed was Mile Gojic. Could you confirm this, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm doing my best to remember exactly what I said about POW Mile Gojic. I do know for sure that I spoke to that man. I was there, and there's a document indicating that. This information was then passed on to the security administration. I do have to point out that I spoke to other POWs as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that same period?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it's very difficult for me. It has been a long time. I can't remember if it was at the same time. But if he was brought in together with a whole group of POWs, then it must have been at the same time. There would have been no reason for me not to if they were all there already, but I do believe that there should exist documents indicating just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One other question still with regard to that POW. During the cross-examination, you were shown a document. I believe it was Exhibit 671, and this document does not show that this prisoner was mistreated. You confirmed that this document does not reveal any mistreatment, nor does it show that he was afraid. Do you remember that this morning?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, during the examination-in-chief, you said that during the interview with that person, you made sure or you verified whether or not he was afraid. Do you remember that? You spoke about what you personally noticed, but I'd like to explore this issue in greater depth. I'd like to know what was exactly was he afraid of?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to be brief. As far as I remember from this place and time, since that interview happened almost 17 -- sorry, 12 or 13 years ago, there were rumours about that unit which caused fear among the members of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I could see the same fear with this prisoner of war. Allegedly, as far as I can recall, these Mujahedin treated their prisoners of war inhumanely, and they applied different types of torture. However, when interviewing this man, he himself stated and said that he received quite a different treatment. Had he mentioned anything concerning any potential torture that he may have undergone, I am convinced that would have been noted down in the report. He expressed some fear based on the rumours of which I knew, too, in Zenica, for example, but I was never able to see that for myself. I don't know whether I was sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sufficiently clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interjecting, Your Honours. It's a matter of translation. On page 39, at line number 4, it's been recorded in the transcript that the witness said: "Allegedly, as far as I can recall, these Mujahedin treated their prisoners of war inhumanely." Madam Vidovic tells me that, in fact, what the witness said is: "Allegedly, as far as the rumours went, those Mujahedin treated their," et cetera. So I don't know whether it's necessary to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the witness is nodding. Can you just say, in words, was mean by your nod, so that it goes on the record, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. Can we have Exhibit 779 on the screen, please. Can we have the last page on both languages, please, the signature page. Can we see the signature page on the English. Sorry. Thank you so much. Sir, there's been a lot of talk about the fact that this document is not signed and that where the author is supposed to have signed, it's crossed out by a line. But there are words in brackets below that, and I would like you to tell me what they signify, where it says: "Certified by signature and stamp."

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can explain that. Below the first and last name and this gentleman's title, since he was supposed to sign the information, the report, it says: "Certified by signature and stamp," which points to the fact that this should have been so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if that had been so, does that make this document a working document or a true document that went out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going by what I can see, I think this is a draft, a working version I prepared myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And a working version that is certified by a stamp and a signature?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not certified. You can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you've just said to me now, when I asked you the question, "What do those words mean," you said it must have been signed and stamped. You said it must have been so.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. It should have been so. I suppose this is a working draft, since there is no full signature by an officer and there is no stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I hear that. I can see there is no signature and I can see there is no stamp. Now, tell me, what do these words mean, the words in brackets?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecutor asked me whether I know what "packet communication" means. In such an encrypted message system, inter alia, in the signature block where the authorised officer was supposed to sign, and in this case it would be Colonel Agan Haseljic, assistant commander for security, it should always be stated that it was certified by signature and stamp. It was an integral part of the system of sending out messages. In the encrypted -- rather, in the packet communication, the person receiving could not receive neither the signature nor the stamp. However, the sender, the person in charge of sending the document, was not allowed to send it without signing it and stamping it first. That's what the thing is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if that is the case, then it means it is a document that did get sent, but it got sent through the encrypted system. Is that what I understand you to say?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me try and clarify. I am not certain whether this document was sent or -- this was a working version. It may have been sent in a different form with a signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me put my question slightly differently. You accept that if the document is sent through encrypted mechanism, the person receiving it will receive a document without a signature and a stamp. Now, if that is the case, and let me just ask, was this document sent by encrypted mechanism, if we look at the first page? Now, can you look at it and tell us whether it was sent by encrypted system? Could we see the full page, the top part of the full page in the Bosnian. Are you able to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I truly cannot discuss here the way of sending documents, especially electronic sending of documents and receiving, since I am very unfamiliar with that field. I suppose, had it been received, there should have been a reception stamp. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I was asking you whether this document, when you look at it, is it a document that was sent by encrypted mechanism? Are you able to say so, or are you not able to say so, sir? Are you able to tell us, by looking at it, whether it was sent by encrypted mechanism?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm anything with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't confirm anything. So if a document sent by encrypted mechanism reaches the addressee without the signature of the author and the stamp, on what basis do you call this a working document? There are two possibilities here: It could be a working document, or it could be a document sent by encrypted mechanism. Now, my question to you is: On what basis do you call this one a working document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my assumption that this is a working version is based on the fact that, in place of the signature block, there is a slash, a line where the signature should have been. We don't have a complete signature, which makes me doubt -- or rather, suspect that this is a working document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you realise that the words in brackets are not crossed out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me turn to another topic. Sir, you were shown documents during cross-examination which were reports coming from the lower units to your unit, mentioning various maltreatments to either prisoners of war or civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask Your Honour to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were shown documents that reported some maltreatment to varying degrees of prisoners of war and civilians, coming from the 35th Division to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never seen, personally, such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You were shown documents from the 3rd Corps, going to the General Staff, which did not mention any maltreatment of the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the professional line of work I performed, I received and I was receiving such documents, but only to the extent of the nature of my work and my need to report on events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you again. You were shown documents that were drafted by you, going to the General Staff, which did not contain everything that you had been told in the reports that you received from the lower units; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything I received from the subordinate unit was included. I endeavoured to include everything to the maximum extent possible, including the part pertaining to any inhumane treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you tell us one inhumane treatment that you included?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of such cases, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll leave, then, that topic. Let me ask you something. The Trial Chamber received evidence from one of the prisoners of war, who told us that you told him virtually what to write in his statement, and specifically told him not to say that the El Mujahedin Detachment maltreated him. Do you have any comments to make on that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that is correct. That was not my modus operandi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. There is testimony to that effect.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irrespective of that, I stand by what I said. I claim that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour, one question arising from Judge Lattanzi's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: With regard to the treatment of Mr. Gojic, you stated that he was treated differently. Well, sir, my question is: Isn't it a possibility that he was treated differently because he claimed he would convert?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific? Where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. Prosecuting counsel earlier on raised an objection about questions which invited the witness to speculate, and I would submit that this is a similar situation. The Prosecuting counsel is asking the witness: "Isn't it a possibility he was treated differently?" It's not inviting him to comment on the facts of he saw or heard. It's speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he claimed that the witness -- his opinion was the witness converted out of fear, and it stems from the witness's own response earlier. So it's a follow-up from that. I can rephrase the question, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's a problem in that that's his opinion, actually. It's not fact. There could be any other or anybody else could have another opinion as to why he converted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions from you, Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, you were asked questions about the document relating to Mile Gojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before we turn to that document, if I could please ask the witness to be shown Exhibit 553, which was shown to the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, do you remember being shown this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can scroll to the bottom in the B/C/S version and go to the second page in the English document.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you could look at the initials in the B/C/S version, you may not be able to see it on this copy here. But if I can pass you the hard copy, am I right in saying that you accepted that you were -- oh, no, there's a comment at the top that -- were you the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's an exhibit already?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's an exhibit, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, what I want to ask you about is: If you can look at the top of the B/C/S version, would you agree with me that here we can see that this document has been sent crypto-protected via the packet communications system?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can scroll to the top in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you see that? You were not able to see it a little earlier when I asked you the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, and that's what I'm trying to explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours how you can tell this has been sent by packet?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. Your Honour, in the upper right-hand corner, there is a rectangular stamp. There, you can see clearly that the document was received, and you can see the last name and the first letter of the name of the operative who received it, the person working with the system. It all points to the fact that this was, indeed, sent via that type of communication. You can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Does it show that it was sent via that type of communication, or does it show that it was received, that stamp? How do I see, from this stamp, that it was sent via that communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have something underlined here inside the stamp. It says: "Received."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But how does that say, therefore, that it was sent via the crypto-protected mechanism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, as far as I can remember, the principle in order was that once a document is received, it had to be received in this specific manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is proof of receipt. It is not proof of the mechanism of sending, and I want to find out. You said, and let me read it to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interject. But this is exactly what I was just going to explore with the witness, so if you perhaps will allow me. If we can go back so we can see the B/C/S version in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Saric, at the top of this document, we can see that there is a heading. There is a bold line which goes horizontally across the page; and at the very, very top of the document, we can see that there's a serial number. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it the case that we can tell that this document was sent by the packet system because there is information above that bold horizontal line, and what we can see there is that there is information about the date that it was sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see any information above the bold line. Can we bring it down?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in the English version as well. It's above the bold line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you called our attention --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've called our attention to the B/C/S side, so I'm looking at it. Anyway, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, obviously the type is a little bit faint on the B/C/S version. It's captured in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Saric, we can see that above that bold line, there is information there, which gives details about a file number, although certainly we can see there's a number "K300M70B." We can see the date the document was sent, the time it was sent, and also there's a number which should be the number of the packet machine that sent this document. Would you agree with me that this is information which shows that this particular document was sent by the packet system?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then you specifically mentioned the stamp which we can see on the right-hand side. You told the Trial Chamber that this indicated it had been received. So somebody had received this from the packet system and stamped it to show receipt. Would you agree with me that "KZ" is an abbreviation which means "crypto-protected"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the stamp is not in the English version, so you've got to look in the B/C/S version, in the top right-hand corner. Perhaps if we could have a close-up again of that stamp, it says "KZ/OSVB3."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, do you know what that means, "KZ/OSVB3, BROJ K"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify for you. I think I do. It is an acronym for "Crypto-protection of the organ of the security service of" probably "the 3rd Corps," "Number," and then "K."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So what we can tell from this document is that the document was sent at a particular time and date; and from the stamp in the right-hand corner, we can see that it was received, and somebody has signed that as sufficient proof. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, finally, if we could please have a look at Exhibit 779, and if we could focus on the top of this document in the B/C/S version, please. Again, if we can just scroll to the top in the English version, just so we can make sure we can see all the information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that on this document, we do not have the horizontal line with all of the information that we could see in the other document, and certainly there's no stamp indicating receipt. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So on the face of this document, as we look at it now, this would indicate that it has not been sent by the packet system?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, sir. That brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. The Chamber takes this opportunity to thank you for coming to testify. You are now excused, and you may stand down. Thank you very much. Travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, Mr. Kyle Wood will be handling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Zaim Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court your name, for the record?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Zaim Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, have you ever testified before in the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In February 2005, I testified in the Hadzihasanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, during 1993, what job did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a military police battalion commander in the 3rd Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Prior to 1993, had you ever had any particular training in regards to military policing?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In the former JNA training system, I had first attended the Reserve Officers College in Bileca, and then I joined the Military Police Training Centre in Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: For how long were you commander of the Military Police Battalion, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of December, 1992, to June 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After 1997, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was in June or July 1997 that I was transferred; and for a while, I served as the Military Police Battalion commander in the General Staff of the BH Army, and then I became deputy commander in that same battalion. Finally, I became deputy commander in the battalion for logistics of the Joint Command of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could I ask you to speak a little more slowly, sir. It looks like the interpreters are struggling to keep pace with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Are you presently in the military, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What rank did you hold in 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Captain, Second Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown what's been marked for identification Exhibit 00817, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, is this document marked for identification as an exhibit already?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's my information that it's been marked for identification as an exhibit, but not yet admitted, Your Honour. Marked for identification 00817 is what I've been told is the proper name for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Not in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what this document is, what affect this document has, what this document is doing, in particular in regard to the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document has not been put on any of the exhibit lists which has been sent to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's an exhibit marked for identification 817. It's already in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. If it's not necessary to put documents marked for identification on the exhibit list, then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If it's a procedural issue, I don't know what the answer is. But I know that previously we've had documents marked for identification, and they've been clearly put upon the exhibit list which has been sent to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit list for a specific witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I was just trying to find in my e-mail, Your Honour. I did notify the Defence that I would be adding this to the exhibit list. We did circulate an exhibit list first. This document came to my attention. I notified them later, via e-mail, that we would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the date of the e-mail, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to confirm. My case manager is looking at that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could assist. I can confirm that we did receive an e-mail on the 15th of November, saying that there was an intention to add the document to the list, but then we subsequently received an updated exhibit list and it made no mention of this particular document. So, really, I think it's just a procedural question for the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not the Prosecution is entitled to use the document with this witness, in that the latest version of the exhibit list did not contain the document on it.
