utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I believe the Defence has been put on sufficient notice that the Prosecution would be showing this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I understand, the argument of the Defence is that the Prosecution, in their e-mail, mentioned the intention to do so, but didn't do so, the intention to add the document, but didn't add it in the updated exhibit list that was sent subsequently to them. Are you able to address that point? That's the point that is being raised with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The subsequent exhibit list that was sent was to make minor corrections to other exhibits. This had not been added to that because I felt it sufficient that I had notified them via e-mail that I would be showing this already. Certainly, it should have been added to that one that was distributed second, but the fact remains this is a document that the Defence is familiar with. This is a document that I specifically told them I would be showing to this witness. I believe they've had sufficient notice for this document to be shown and for this witness to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the wording of the e-mail? We haven't got this e-mail now. You're saying the e-mail mentioned the intention to send you this document or to send it as a list, or I'm not quite sure what your e-mail said. I'm not sure whether the e-mail was telling you specifically that the Prosecution is going to use this document, or what did it tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the e-mail in front of me, and it says: "I write to inform you that I am adding PT2797 to the exhibit list for Zaim Mujezinovic, whose name appears in this document." That was on the 15th, and then I believe it was either yesterday, or the day before, we received the revised exhibit list. It didn't contain it. I mean, all I can say is that when we receive these revised exhibit lists, it's common for documents to drop out and for new documents to go in. But, generally, we take it or understand it that that is the final version, listing the documents the Prosecution will use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the e-mail says: "I'm writing to inform you that I am adding this to the exhibit list," I don't know what need there is still. It doesn't tell you of an intention to do so. It tells you that it is doing so, and that's probably the reason they didn't add it in the subsequent list, because they told themselves they'd notified you of it already. Now, I don't know. You see, the internal workings of how you give each other notice, the Chamber is not very familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As I say, normally it's understood that the final version of the exhibit list that's sent to us will contain all the documents to be used with a particular witness in court. If you believe that the Prosecution has given sufficient notice, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, from the wording of this e-mail, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be easier if we just moved to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I draw your attention particularly to the second-to-last name written in bold there. Whose name is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what is the rank that's listed for you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Senior Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you had a chance to look at this document, the first page of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We didn't. We would like to see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. If we could go back to the first page, so we can see from the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Scroll down the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can see, for example, that this says "Order," commending individuals listed below. The list continues on to the second page, where you said your name appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you remember being commended for your acts or your activities in December 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. There was an order on my commendation. I got it as a document of the 3rd Corps, but this probably followed the original order written by the command of the BH Army -- of the General Staff of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if we go to the second page just one last time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, can you see whose name appears to have signed this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And do you recognise that signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You assume that you recognise it? The question was: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers this exhibit into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. I guess it will stay as Exhibit number 817.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mujezinovic, I want to ask you some more questions about the Military Police Battalion. Could you please explain to the Court, who was your superior in 1993, as a commander of the Military Police Battalion in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I was the MP Battalion commander. My direct superior was the corps commander. That was General Enver Hadzihasanovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Who was your direct superior in 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: My direct superior, the corps commander, was General Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, as a Military Police Battalion commander, did you report to anybody else in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the rules governing the military police, the MP Battalion commander had the responsibility of reporting to the organ in the 3rd Corps Command that was their technical superior; organ, in this case, chief of the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And who was that person in 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But from the time the corps was set up, the sequence of chiefs was as follows: Tadija Brekalo, Agic Nasib, Ramiz Dugalic, Ekrem Alihodzic, Agan Haseljic; and, finally, when the corps ceased to exist, the acting chief was Muharem Zijaja [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise to deal with a matter of translation, and I believe it will be cropping up quite frequently during the course of this witness's testimony. At page 60, line 10, the witness referred to a "technical superior." I'm informed that the better translation is "professional superior." This is a point that has cropped up previously during the course of the hearing. I wonder, maybe this should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any comment to make, Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Certainly, I have no comment about whether the translation is proper or correct, Your Honour. I can indicate that I will get into this more fully with the next document that I intend to show the witness. Perhaps this will shed light on the question. From what I understand, "professionally" is probably acceptable, but that's something for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, is it technically or professionally, this person who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert, expert superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, if I may help, in the French translation, the term "professional" was used as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I think this might be cleared up as soon as I show the next document, Your Honour. So if the witness could be shown that, Exhibit -- I'm sorry, document P04054.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, do you see that document, the first page of that document, on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And we see in the English that it says: "The Rules of Service for the Military Police of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Are these the rules that you used during your career as the commander of the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Especially in light of the confusion that arose earlier, if I could have the witness shown page 8 in the Bosnian version and page 7 in the English version. As the computer gets there, I can tell Defence and the Chamber that I'm particularly looking at 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In particular, especially in light of the confusion about whether "technical" or "professional" is correct, I would draw your attention to paragraph 8, Mr. Witness. Does this paragraph fully explain how it is that you had what amounts to two superiors as a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The chapter is entitled "Command and Control Over and Military Police." This defines the relations in the command-and-control system, the relations that prevailed within that system. If you read paragraph seven, which reads: "The military police is commanded and controlled by the senior officer of the military unit or institution incorporating the unit of the military police, to which it is attached." So what that means is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What that means is my superior, in that sense, is the commander of the 3rd Corps, the superior of the MP Battalion. If you look at paragraph 8, it defines the subordination or superior status in professional or technical terms, which means that the superior of the Military Police Battalion was the chief of the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I interrupt? Not you, Witness; I want to interrupt the interpretation. I don't see an alternative in paragraph 8, but the interpretation says "professional or technical terms," and we are trying to resolve this difference between "professional" and "technical." Can we stay with one term, please, interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. The term I see on paragraph 8 is "professional." I don't see "technical." Okay. Thank you, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers this exhibit into -- or this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object to it going in with it being an exhibit, but I'm told by Madam Vidovic that this is already in evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It may be 586. It may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 586. Yes. I think we have referred to this document several times. If the Registrar could help us check 586, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: As I understand it, Your Honour, only certain pages of it are admitted into evidence. I will be asking the witness more questions about this document. I believe it's appropriate at this point that the entire document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just find out what 586 contains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is being advised that Exhibit 586 is the entire document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to place on record what to do with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: As long as it's in evidence as Exhibit 586 -- do I have that number right? Is it 586?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll refer to that instead, and perhaps it would be best if 586 be brought up itself document P04054.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please have 586 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And as that is coming up, I do have some more questions for the witness that is aside from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, you've told us that you were the commander of the Military Police Battalion in the 3rd Corps. If you could please tell the Trial Chamber, what other military police formations were there in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of establishment, the military police units that were within the 3rd Corps were categorised as follows: There were platoons that existed within 3rd Corps brigades; then there were military police companies in the brigades, I'm sorry, mechanised ones, motorised ones; and operations groups and divisions that were part of the 3rd Corps as well. Directly within the 3rd Corps Command, there was the MP Battalion, of which I was commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem here. I'm sorry. I have a problem when certain expressions are being used. Up to now, we've been talking of the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion. During this trial, during the testimonies that we've heard during this trial, we have heard "Military Police Service" within the 3rd Corps. So I want to be clear about how things are called. The entity you were aware of, was it a military police battalion of the 3rd Corps, or was it a military police service, or was it a military police unit of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of formation, it was called "Battalion of the Military Police of the 3rd Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I do have some questions that will probably illuminate this issue a little more, Your Honour. I take note of the time. Is it an appropriate time for the Court to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed, if it is convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, just before the break, Mr. Mujezinovic, we were discussing the various units and exactly what "military police service" meant, rather than "military police battalion." Given that most of us in the room, and perhaps watching, aren't experts on the military formations, and so on, it might be helpful for you to explain, for example, what exactly is a military police battalion and what its strength would be, what a platoon would be and its strength, and a company and what it's strength would be in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: A military police battalion is an establishment structure comprising the following elements: The MP Battalion Command, the platoon in charge of military police investigations, two military police companies, one traffic and one logistics company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how many men would be in a battalion at full strength, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Around 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How many men would be in a platoon at full strength?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: A platoon would have between 30 and 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How many men would be in a company at full strength?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Between 80 and 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned, in your answer before, that the brigades, for example, would have a military police formation. What would be the strength of the formation of the military police unit at a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In infantry and similar brigades, military police units were organised as military police platoons. As for motorised or mechanised brigades, military police units were organised into companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was there a military police unit that was typically assigned to a unit that had the strength of a detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, there was no need to organise military police units within detachments. Should the situation in the field require such a thing, and if the superior commander assessed that a part of the military police should be resubordinated to the detachment, it was possible, in view of the establishment, but a separate order was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In order to understand the relationship between the Military Police Battalion and those units on the brigade level and lower, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what, if any, command-and-control authority you had, as commander of the Military Police Battalion, over the units in the brigades, for example, the military police units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely none. The Military Police Battalion commander could only command those units and officers which were a part of his own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, we discussed a little bit earlier a document that has subsequently been identified as Exhibit 586.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I wonder if 586 could be brought up again on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's on the screen already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see that it is. I was watching the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, I know this is a different form than what I showed you, but does this appear to be the rule book governing your operations during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I can only see the cover page, and there is nothing that can be in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Perhaps if we move forward in the document a little bit, maybe two or three pages. That's probably sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, seeing this document, does this look like the book that you used as a military police battalion commander during 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it looks that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what does this book say about the role of the military police, in terms of crime prevention and detection?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Here, we have a narrow definition of the assignments of military police units within the area that is under their control, defining their obligation to undertake measures and procedures with a view of preventing certain criminal activities and to physically secure the command post and other vital elements within the system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What role, specifically, did the military police have in investigating crimes, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: For example, one thing that was done by the Military Police Battalion, in terms of investigations, is as follows: When information is received on a crime committed in a certain area, the duty service of the MP Battalion notifies the competent investigative military judge and sends out a patrol to the scene. At the scene, the police patrol cordons the area off; that is, the area where it is believed that the crime had been committed. They also conduct interviews with eyewitnesses, if any, and they gather other evidence on the alleged offence. Once the military investigative judge is present, he takes over of all investigating procedures and activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is that where the role of the military police ends in the investigation of a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What role, specifically, did the Military Police Battalion have in investigating crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The same as the one I've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps is also the area of responsibility of the military police of the 3rd Corps. I also have to say that lower-ranking units, that of brigades and divisions, had their own respective zones. The territorial competence, in terms of investigating, was with the units of the military police within those brigades or divisions active in the area. The Military Police Battalion was used in such activities to assist, or if those units which have the territorial competence, and I mean the military police, are not equipped sufficiently. In that case, the battalion would undertake the whole investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Speaking of the military police, in general, was there any other organ in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had jurisdiction or authority to investigate crimes committed by ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no special organised unit which could investigate such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, then, the primary responsibility for investigating crimes rested with the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, referring to the document before you again, what does that document say about the role of the military police in dealing with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The military police is tasked with transporting prisoners of war from the unit which had captured them to the Reception Centre for Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what does the rule book say, the document in front of you, what does it say about the role of the military police in military discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The military police, as well as all other organs of command and control, were tasked to ensure that at their respective levels of duties and obligations, to carry out control of the implementation of the military disciplinary measures prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown document P02749, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, do you see that document in front of you, or the first page of that document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And could you please tell the Court whose signature that is at the bottom of this first page?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now if we could move to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I'll ask, Mr. Mujezinovic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this document in its original regarding this period; however, in terms of content and form, I believe it is authentic. The role of the document was to clarify the role of military police units in implementing prescribed military disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 in the B/C/S, and that is page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll draw your attention, in particular, to the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I guess we're already on page 2 in the B/C/S, but page 4 in the English, the second paragraph, which explains that the military police had a specific obligation to submit disciplinary reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is that consistent with what you recall of your obligations during 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The procedure was as follows: In situations in which a military police patrol from the 3rd Corps or an authorised official, or whoever it was that was in the field and was a member of the battalion, realises that there was a breach in terms of military discipline, the Military Police Battalion submits a report to the commander of the unit from which the person who had committed the crime is. That is where our duties cease, and the commander of that unit is the only person responsible to implement disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And was there a similar rule book that governed military discipline in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, generally speaking, sir, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether what's written in this document, that is, P02749, does this accurately reflect the proper procedure for military discipline in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I focused only on the obligations of the units of the military police. This document includes a more detailed instruction on the implementing of the measures pertaining to military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers document P02749 into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P02749 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, continuing on the issue of military discipline, if a soldier had been found to have assaulted a prisoner of war, would that have been a matter for military discipline or the military courts?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the degree of the assault or maltreatment. If it entails criminal responsibility, it cannot be seen as a breach of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If a soldier under the jurisdiction of the military police had been found to have murdered a prisoner of war, would that have been a matter for military discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. There is criminal liability entailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just following up on your previous answer about assault, how serious would the assault have to be for it to be a criminal matter versus merely a disciplinary matter?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I am not a lawyer. However, I know that the law defines types of criminal responsibility, and we also have military disciplinary measures and responsibility defined; therefore, that is all I can tell you, in terms of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could I have the witness be shown Exhibit P01052, please -- or document P01052.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I draw your attention particularly to the second bullet point under ordinal number 1. Mr. Mujezinovic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember it from the date when it was created; but as part of these proceedings, I remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And focusing on that second bullet point, where it mentions: "Instigate disciplinary proceedings against all perpetrators of disciplinary violations at the 3rd Corps Military Disciplinary Court." Can we conclude, from this document, that the Military Disciplinary Court was functioning at this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We can conclude that there was a military disciplinary court at the level of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers P01052 into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P01052 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 868.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit more about the functioning of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If document P01893 could please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So we can see from the document, sir, that this says: "3rd Corps Military Police Battalion." Was this a document that was produced by the unit of which you were the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of content and form, this document corresponds to the documents produced by us. It was signed by an authorised official from the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, I see that at the top it says "Official Note." Can you explain to the Trial Chamber when a document like this, called an Official Note, would have been produced?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In cases when we have gathered certain information from any source which, in our view, could be treated by the military police, then such an Official Note is drafted as a first step.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And to whom is such an Official Note directed? Who is it sent to?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The note is sent to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers P01893 into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P01893 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 869.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Next, could the witness be shown document P01990, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see that document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And is this similar to the document we saw before? This one says -- it's been translated into English as "Official Record." Is it the same as an Official Note that would have been produced when a particular incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same type of document, the same title, "Official Note," and the procedure is the same as in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So we can see from the document that on 19 March 1995, the El Mujahedin Detachment security organ passed on information that one civilian person was creating problems. Can we conclude from this, sir, that the security organ of the El Mujahedin Detachment called on the Military Police Battalion for assistance in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We can conclude that the patrol of the military police attended the scene following a request made by an official from the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And why wouldn't the El Mujahid Detachment's own military police unit have handled this situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a leading question. We've heard no evidence from this witness that the El Mujahedin Detachment had its own military police unit. It's been suggested that there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did the El Mujahedin Detachment have its own military police unit, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Neither the El Mujahedin Detachment nor the other detachments within the ABiH did not have military police units, in terms of establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So if they had a problem that called for the use of military police, who would they have to rely upon?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There were two mechanisms they could rely on. The first one was by contacting directly the duty officer of the Military Police Battalion, which operated around the clock, in case of similar situations, and the same goes for units and civilians. The other would be to follow it up the chain of control and command and to notify the person in charge of security in the unit, who would then contact the chief of security of the 3rd Corps and request that the Military Police Battalion be sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interject, Mr. Wood. Sir, did the El Mujahedin Detachment have a security organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As per establishment, in detachments, there were assistant commanders for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to answer my question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The El Mujahedin Detachment had a security organ through the security system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Where would this document have been sent, this Official Record?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: To the Military Security Sector of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers document P01990 into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P01990 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 870.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown document P02335, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, while we're waiting, Mr. Mujezinovic, I see that in your last answer, at page 77, line 9, you say: "... to the Military Security Sector of the 3rd Corps." Now, it's just a matter of terminology, but is "Military Security Sector" the same as "Military Security Service"?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The service is a broader concept, and the sector is a narrower form of organisation, but it's the same organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, turning to the document in front of you, sir, do you recognise this document or at least the form of it?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the format.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of the B/C/S version, the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: There's a signature there, sir. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, going back to the first page - and I apologise for whipsawing us back and forth here - but going back to the first page, you say you recognised the format. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what this report is and how often you would write reports like this?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion had to report on a monthly basis to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps on all of its activities, including any criminal reports filed over that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, looking at that part, in particular at the bottom of the page, we see there, under the "Criminal Code of the Republic of BiH": Article 181, Endangering public traffic; Article 217, Forging documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This list goes on to the second page if we could show that, the subsequent page, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Taking a look at that list, sir, would you characterise this particular report for this particular month as characteristic of the types of criminal activities and reports that you would file or that were filed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The number of criminal reports is average, and this is more or less the procedure that we followed for all our criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you say "criminal reports," what would constitute a criminal report? Would that be a report that was simply drafted or one that was sent on further down the line?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that was simply drafted, documented, and forwarded to the relevant court for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, the cases that are noted in this table, these refer -- do these refer to criminal reports that had been drafted and forwarded to the appropriate criminal court?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where would this -- where did you send these reports to, after you drafted them, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Having drafted these criminal reports, they would be forwarded to the appropriate court. A copy would also be forwarded to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Perhaps you misunderstood my question. This particular document that we're looking at here, after you drafted this document, where would you have sent it?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: To the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers document P02335 into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P02335 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 871.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown document P02531, document P02531. If we could see the end of this document, the final page of it in the Bosnian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, do you see that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, we can see from the document that your name is typed, but then the word "Za" is written and then there's a signature. Is this your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And do you know who it was who signed this?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my memory, I assume it to have been Dzemal Muharemovic, who was one of the company commanders. I was probably away, and he was authorised to sign documents on behalf of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Let's move to the first page and have a look at the document in closer detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll ask first, Mr. Mujezinovic: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but the format is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just glancing over it, and knowing the circumstances in which it was signed and so on, do you have any reason to doubt its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Prosecution offers document P02531 into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P02531 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I want to move to a different area now, Mr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In doing that, I would like the witness to please be shown document P02479.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, do you recognise this document or at least the format of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise the format. This is a report by the Military Police Battalion, sent to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I see, at least in the English, it says "Daily Report." Is that reflective of how often the report would have been filed with the Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The MP Battalion was supposed to send daily, weekly, and monthly reports to the Military Security Service. Whenever this was required, there were also interim reports about some special circumstances occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, there's a -- you mentioned earlier that one of the obligations of the Military Police Battalion was to secure facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: To secure vital facilities, those vital to the command-and-control system of the 3rd Corps. So the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, in this document, sir, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what is mentioned about the activities of the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion in securing any facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the MP Battalion, based on this report at least, was securing the command post of the 3rd Corps, but it was also patrolling alongside with a military police company belonging to the 35th Division. That's in the first section, which talks about the crucial tasks or activities, or main tasks. It talks about certain activities. That's what this report reflects.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention in particular to item A, where in the English it says: "The unit focuses its activity on the zone of responsibility," and then it ends with, "in the sector of Luke village." Is this the command post that you are speaking of that the Military Police Battalion was in charge of securing?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The MP Battalion did one thing: It physically secured the command post of the 3rd Corps. There was no other form of activity, because there was the MP company that was territorially in charge of other things. The only thing that this unit did was to physically secure the command post of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you say "the command post of the 3rd Corps," are you referring, sir, to what is in this document, in the sector of Luke village?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers document P02479 into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P02479 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 873.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. I'm moving now into an area that involves some protected witnesses. I will endeavour not to say their names, so if the next document could be exhibited under seal. If the Trial Chamber believes that we go into private session, I'm at your discretion for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Wood, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could move to Exhibit -- or document P02681.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recognise the form of this document, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when would a document like this have been produced?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: When these persons were being brought in - and this is something that the military police could do for a variety of reasons - on such occasions, a document is produced that is normally described as a transfer list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could just clear up one thing. If you could explain to the Trial Chamber what the initials "CZPRZ" at the top of the Bosnian version of this document is.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: "POW Reception Centre." That is the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document 2681 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 875.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I have one final document to show. That is document P02721. Perhaps we need to see the second page of the B/C/S, if there is one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, do you recognise the form of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And under what circumstances would this sort of document have been produced?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: When there is a hand-over of POWs, or other persons from the units that the person who had committed a crime comes from, in that case the military police would first draft a report on the hand-over, and they should also include a full list as well as the route to be taken. That should be concluded with an Official Note, and the report submitted to the security organ of the 3rd Corps, so the Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whose signature is at the bottom right-hand portion of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It is rather illegible, but I believe it could be Zakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And the signature on the other -- directly across from that, on the left -- lower left-hand side of the document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I see that it says "Aiman."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And according to this format and to the procedures, who is the person who would have signed that portion of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The left or the right one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The left side.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The person who is commanding the unit can authorise someone to carry out the hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So when you say "unit," that would mean, in this context, the unit in whose custody the POWs are before the hand-over?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers document P02721 into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document P02721 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit number 876.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I just have a few more questions, Mr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: As a member of the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion, did you ever receive any information about murders that took place in a place called "Bikosi"?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you ever receive information, in your capacity as commander of the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion, about the mistreatment of POWs in a place called "Livade" or what's referred to as "the Kamenica camp"?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mujezinovic. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'm representing General Delic. I'll be asking you some questions. So, Mr. Mujezinovic, the background to your military career is that in April 1992, you became the commander of a military police platoon within the Zenica District Defence Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then, in September 1992, you were promoted to commander of a military police company within the Zenica District Defence Staff; and then, finally, in December 1992, you became the commander of the Military Police Battalion within the 3rd Corps. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Turning to the time that you became the commander of the Military Police Battalion within the 3rd Corps, is it right that in December 1992, the Military Police Battalion was actually established at that point, and effectively it started from scratch?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. There was an order by the commander of the 3rd Corps forming the Military Police Battalion. It was a brand-new unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it was a brand-new unit. Is it right that there was no structure in place; and then, over a period of time, the structure was established that you told us about today: The battalion command, the two companies, the traffic section, logistics, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It took quite some time for the unit to become harmonised with the regulation that was in place, due to a number of circumstances that were in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned it took some time for the unit to become harmonised with the regulation that was in place. The regulation that you're referring to is the Rules of Service for the Military Police of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I meant to say that it be harmonised with the prescribed establishment; however, the rule book defines our sphere of activity. When I say "to harmonise it with establishment," it should include that the order of the command of the 3rd Corps defines the structure. Therefore, through a Defence office, we had to secure personnel and equipment, so that we could fit the battalion within the existing establishment. When such establishment is put in place, preconditions are met, so that the battalion can actually follow the rule book on the work of a military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it correct that the Military Police Battalion was constantly evolving throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The MP Battalion suffered, so to say, at least three to four changes in terms of establishment. Usually, such recommendation was made with a view to trying to reconcile that with the situation and possibilities that existed in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that, even by the very end of the war, the Military Police Battalion had still not established all of the functions that it was required to have to meet the needs set down by the rules of service for the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The MP Battalion, from the very first moment until the end, never managed to fulfill the preconditions, in terms of establishment, 100 per cent. Primarily, I mean the equipment, since circumstances were such, and the army existed within those circumstances. What was particularly lacking was anti-sabotage equipment, documentation means, and other regulation of establishing responsibility; for example, to take fingerprints, et cetera. There were also personnel problems, since within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no institutions in place, in the sense that personnel was not particularly or specifically educated to perform the tasks of military police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So just to pick upon one of the points you mentioned, the Military Police Battalion lacked the technical means to discharge its duties properly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that the Military Police Battalion was staffed by members that lacked proper training and experience to properly carry out the role as a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The principle of bringing up to strength depended much on any previous experience when military police was engaged. It all had to go through the competent defence office. We could also request that personnel changes be made within the 3rd Corps, so as to get people from other units which had certain officers with a degree of military police knowledge. Another way would be to educate the existing personnel, following the instruction and curriculum of the security sector of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in general terms, can you tell us, if at all possible, when the Military Police Battalion was formed in December 1992, what sort of proportion of the members of the battalion had some sort of relevant previous experience or training?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to address that in general terms. However, I dare say that there were very few people, especially officers, who had had any sort of knowledge or experience in military police work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, we haven't finished with you. If you could please come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Court will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
